summary: This Informational document defines a number of keywords and mailbox name attributes already used across server and client implementations, describes their intended use, and registers them with IANA to avoid name collisions.

plainLanguage.summary: Email programs already use some special labels. This writes them down in one place so nobody uses the same name for different things.

subtitle: Standardized labels for email features that were already in wide use

tldr.problem: Email clients and servers were already using keywords like $hasattachment and $muted, but they had no official registry, risking name collisions and inconsistent behavior.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC formally defines 17 new message keywords and 3 mailbox attributes, then registers them with IANA to prevent conflicts and ensure all implementations understand them the same way.
tldr.outcome: Email systems can now reliably share structured information about messages (whether they have attachments, if the user muted the thread, if it was auto-sent) across different email providers and clients.

today: RFC 9979 is an Informational RFC providing official definitions and IANA registrations for email keywords and mailbox attributes already in use. It has not been obsoleted and remains the standard reference for these features across IMAP and JMAP implementations.

sections.title: The Problem of Informal Keywords
sections.content:
The IMAP standard allows mail servers and clients to mark messages with custom keywords, and many implementations added their own keywords for features. For example, Gmail used $hasattachment to mark messages with file attachments, Apple Mail used $muted for threads the user wanted to silence, and others created their own variants. Without an official registry, there was a risk of collision: two vendors might use the same keyword name for different purposes.

This document takes 17 keywords and 3 mailbox attributes that were already in wide use across major email systems—Gmail, Apple Mail, Fastmail, and others—and gives them official definitions and an IANA registration. This ensures future compatibility and consistency across the email ecosystem.
sections.plainLanguage: Email companies were making up their own labels for message features, but without telling everyone what each label means. This document officially names them so there's no confusion.

sections.title: Message Keywords and Their Uses
sections.content:
The 17 keywords fall into logical groups. Flag colors ($MailFlagBit0, $MailFlagBit1, $MailFlagBit2) combine into a 3-bit pattern encoding seven colors (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, gray) for flagged messages, letting users visually prioritize messages. Attachment detection ($hasattachment, $hasnoattachment) lets clients show a paperclip icon without parsing the entire message, and they are mutually exclusive.

Memo support ($memo, $hasmemo) enables notes-to-self: a user can create a private annotation about a message, stored with the $memo keyword, while the original message gets $hasmemo so clients know an annotation exists. These are mutually exclusive. Subscription management ($canunsubscribe, $unsubscribed) help with mailing list handling: $canunsubscribe means the server found a valid one-click unsubscribe link, while $unsubscribed marks messages from lists the user tried to leave.

Thread management ($followed, $muted) are mutually exclusive and affect how future messages in the thread are handled. $followed signals interest and may trigger special handling (higher priority, notifications), while $muted deprioritizes the thread. Other keywords include $autosent (system-generated messages), $imported (data migrations), $istrusted (server verified the sender), $maskedemail (received via a privacy alias), $new (should be prominent to the user), and $notify (show a notification).
sections.plainLanguage: The keywords label messages for different purposes: colors, file attachments, user notes, unsubscribe info, thread interest level, system messages, and notifications. Each keyword has a clear, single meaning so all email programs understand it the same way.

sections.title: Mailbox Name Attributes
sections.content:
The three mailbox name attributes standardize special-purpose folders. The Snoozed attribute identifies a mailbox where messages are temporarily hidden and scheduled to reappear (e.g., in the inbox) at a future time. When a user snoozes a message, the server moves it here and sets a wake-up time; the $new keyword marks it when it returns.

Scheduled marks a mailbox for drafted messages awaiting a scheduled send time. A user can compose a message and set it to send tomorrow at 9 AM; the server stores it here until the time comes, letting the user review or cancel before sending.

Memos identifies the folder where user-created memo messages (marked with $memo) are stored, separating annotations from regular messages and allowing clients to display them contextually (attached to the message being annotated) rather than as standalone emails.
sections.plainLanguage: These are special mailboxes for messages waiting to reappear later, messages waiting to be sent later, and personal notes attached to other messages. The names tell email programs what each folder is for.

sections.title: Rules for Safe Use
sections.content:
The RFC includes important constraints. The three flag color keywords MUST be ignored if the \Flagged system flag is not set; they are only meaningful on explicitly flagged messages. Clients MUST clear all three when unflagging a message. Mutually exclusive keywords ($hasattachment / $hasnoattachment, $memo / $hasmemo, $followed / $muted) must not both appear on the same message.

For thread-aware keywords like $followed and $muted, the RFC defines thread membership using RFC 8474 (IMAP) and RFC 8621 (JMAP) standards, so different clients agree on which messages belong to the same conversation. The $muted keyword has a security note: if an attacker compromises a user's account, they could mute important threads to hide notifications; however, a compromised account already allows many similar actions, so this risk is proportional.

When using JMAP (the JSON mail protocol), the same keywords apply, with equivalences defined (e.g., JMAP's hasAttachment property must match the $hasattachment keyword).
sections.plainLanguage: Color keywords only work on flagged messages. Some labels can't both be on the same message. Threads are defined the same way across all programs. If someone hacks your email account, they could hide important messages, so be careful.

sections.title: IANA Registration and Future Use
sections.content:
All 17 keywords and 3 mailbox attributes are now registered in IANA registries, preventing future conflicts. The document also defines deprecated alias names (e.g., application/x-protobuf is deprecated in favor of application/protobuf) to support legacy systems.

This is an Informational RFC reflecting IETF consensus. It has not been obsoleted and provides the official reference for these keywords and attributes. Email implementers should check this RFC when adding support for email features that other clients already use, ensuring compatibility and consistency across the ecosystem.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA (the authority that manages internet names) now has an official list of these email labels. If someone invents a new label, they have to check IANA first to make sure the name isn't already taken.

left.title: Has Attachment
left.desc: Message contains one or more file attachments.

right.title: Has No Attachment
right.desc: Message has been analyzed and contains no attachments.
